content: The text provided is a dense and highly detailed compilation of study summaries, outcomes, and comparisons related to the timing of complementary feeding (CF) in infants. 1. Rathnayake (2013) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Sri Lanka involving 1,087 preschool children. The study examined the initiation of complementary feeding after six months in both formula-fed and breastfed infants, with a focus on outcomes related to overweight and obesity. 2. Rippey (2020) performed a prospective cohort study in the United States with 2,794 infants. The study compared formula-fed and breastfed infants introduced to complementary feeding at ≤6 months versus ≥6 months, assessing morbidity outcomes. 3. Robinson (2009) carried out a prospective cohort study in the United Kingdom with 536 children. The study investigated the age of solid food introduction (up to 3, 4, 5 months, and >5 months) in breastfed and non-breastfed children, with body composition measured using DXA scans. 4. Salahuddin (2017) conducted a prospective cohort study in the United States involving 4,497 infants. The study focused on the introduction of complementary foods before four months in breastfed infants and its association with BMI z-scores. 5. Škledar (2015) performed a prospective cohort study in Croatia with 302 healthy Caucasian children. The study examined the introduction of complementary foods before six months in breastfed infants and its relationship with overweight and obesity. 6. Thorisdottir (2019) conducted a prospective cohort study in Iceland with 250 Icelandic infants. The study assessed the introduction of solid foods before four months, noting a high breastfeeding initiation rate (99%) and continued breastfeeding in 88% of infants at the time of solid food introduction. The study also evaluated IgE sensitization. 7. Vadiveloo (2019) carried out a prospective cohort study in the United States with 449 women. The study compared complementary feeding introduced before four months versus at or after four months in infants not exclusively breastfed or formula-fed, focusing on weight-for-length z-scores and healthy food scores. 8. Werdani (2019) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Indonesia with 162 mothers and their toddlers (aged 6–59 months). The study compared complementary feeding introduced before six months versus at or after six months, with malnutrition as the primary outcome. 9. Fauzia (2019) examined dental health outcomes in children aged up to 59 months, focusing on decayed, extracted, or filled tooth surfaces (defs score) and the timing of complementary feeding introduction. 10. Gupta (2017) investigated neurodevelopmental outcomes in infants introduced to complementary feeding at four months versus six months. Outcomes included motor and mental developmental quotients (MoDQ and MeDQ) and their respective centiles. 11. Dewey (1998, 2004) studied motor milestone achievements (e.g., raising the head, rolling over, crawling) in infants introduced to complementary feeding at different ages (e.g., four months versus six months). 12. Various observational studies compared early introduction of complementary feeding (<3, <4, or <6 months) to later introduction (≥3, ≥4, or ≥6 months) in normal-term and preterm infants. Outcomes assessed included growth parameters (e.g., weight, height, BMI), nutritional status (e.g., anemia, iron deficiency), and health conditions (e.g., diarrhea, respiratory illnesses, atopic dermatitis). 13. Late introduction of complementary feeding (>6 or >8 months) was compared to earlier introduction (≤6 or ≤8 months) in normal-term and preterm infants. Outcomes included stunting, underweight, wasting, anemia, and other health indicators. 14. The studies highlighted potential risks and benefits associated with the timing of complementary feeding, emphasizing the importance of individualized approaches based on infant health, growth, and developmental needs. 15. Methodological limitations, such as small sample sizes, risk of bias, and lack of control for confounding factors, were noted in several studies, leading to downgrading of evidence quality in some cases.
